name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Rearranging zones of root in vertical section

questiontext.text:
Rearrange the following zones as seen in the root in vertical section and choose the correct option.

A. Root hair zone
B. Zone of meristems
C. Rootcap zone
D. Zone of maturation
E. Zone of elongation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A growing root tip exhibits distinct anatomical zones arranged sequentially from the apex (distal tip) toward the base (proximal region) as cells are formed, elongate, and differentiate.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the extreme apex lies the protective rootcap zone (C). Immediately above it is the zone of meristems (B), where cells divide actively. Above the meristematic region is the zone of elongation (E), where newly formed cells increase in length. Above this lies the root hair zone (A), where epidermal cells form root hairs for absorption, leading into the fully differentiated zone of maturation (D).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of root zones from the apex upward in a vertical section is C, B, E, A, D.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Position of youngest floral bud in acropetal succession

questiontext.text: In an inflorescence where flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession, the position of the youngest floral bud in the floral axis shall be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a racemose inflorescence, the main floral axis continues to grow indefinitely and bears flowers laterally in an acropetal succession.

Step 2: Evaluation
Acropetal succession means that the oldest flowers are located toward the base (proximal end) of the floral axis, while progressively younger flowers and the youngest floral buds develop toward the growing apex (distal end).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The position of the youngest floral bud in an acropetal inflorescence is distal.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Absence of endosperm in mature gram and pea seeds

questiontext.text: The mature seeds of plants such as gram and peas, possess no endosperm, because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In angiosperms, double fertilization produces both a diploid zygote and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into nutritive endosperm tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gram and peas are dicotyledonous angiosperms in which double fertilization occurs normally and endosperm is formed. However, during seed maturation, the developing embryo completely consumes the endosperm and stores food reserves in the cotyledons, resulting in non-endospermic (exalbuminous) mature seeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mature seeds of gram and peas lack endosperm because the endosperm gets used up by the developing embryo during seed development.

answer.text: There is no double fertilization in them
Endosperm gets used up by the developing embryo during seed development

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Roots developed from parts other than radicle

questiontext.text: Roots developed from parts of the plant other than radicle are called

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Root systems in plants are classified based on their site of origin during development.

Step 2: Evaluation
Taproots arise directly from the elongation of the radicle, and fibrous roots replace a short-lived primary root from the base of the stem in monocots. Roots that originate from any plant part other than the radicle, such as stems or leaves (seen in grass, Monstera, and banyan trees), are termed adventitious roots. Nodular roots are roots containing nitrogen-fixing nodules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Roots developed from parts of the plant other than the radicle are called adventitious roots.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Definition of venation in leaf lamina

questiontext.text: Venation is a term used to describe the pattern of arrangement of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In leaf morphology, vascular strands extend through the expanded green part of the leaf called the lamina (leaf blade).

Step 2: Evaluation
The arrangement of veins and veinlets within the lamina of a leaf is called venation (commonly reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots). The arrangement of floral organs is described by aestivation or floral symmetry, while the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called inflorescence.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Venation describes the pattern of arrangement of veins and veinlets in a lamina.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Absence of endosperm in orchid seeds

questiontext.text: Endosperm, a product of double fertilization in angiosperms is absent in the seeds of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Angiosperm seeds are categorized as endospermic (albuminous) when endosperm persists in the mature seed, or non-endospermic (exalbuminous) when endosperm is absent at maturity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Seeds of coconut, maize, and castor retain endosperm at maturity and are endospermic. Although orchids are monocotyledons, their seeds are non-endospermic and lack endosperm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Endosperm is absent in the seeds of orchids.

questiontext.text: Many pulses of daily use belong to one of the families below (tick the correct answer)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant families are characterized by distinct floral features and include economically important crops such as cereals, pulses, and vegetables.

Step 2: Evaluation
The family Fabaceae (formerly Papilionoideae, a subfamily of Leguminosae) includes major pulses of daily use such as gram, arhar, sem, moong, and soyabean. Solanaceae includes potato and tomato, Liliaceae includes ornamental and medicinal plants like Aloe and tulip, and Poaceae includes cereals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Many pulses of daily use belong to the family Fabaceae.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Attachment of placenta to developing seed

questiontext.text: The placenta is attached to the developing seed near the

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A dicotyledonous seed develops from a fertilized ovule that was attached to the placenta inside the ovary via a stalk called the funicle.

Step 2: Evaluation
The hilum is a scar on the seed coat (testa) marking the point where the funicle attached the developing seed to the fruit and placenta. The micropyle is a small pore above the hilum, and the chalaza is the basal part of the ovule opposite the micropyle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The placenta is attached to the developing seed near the hilum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Plant used to extract blue dye

questiontext.text: Which of the following plants is used to extract the blue dye?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Members of the family Fabaceae have diverse economic uses, including fodder, ornaments, medicines, and natural dyes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Indigofera (specifically Indigofera tinctoria) is a leguminous plant used to extract the natural blue dye indigo. Trifolium is used as fodder, Lupin is grown as an ornamental plant, and Cassia is known for ornamental and medicinal uses.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Indigofera is used to extract the blue dye.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCHING_Q10 - Matching seed and fruit structures with features

questiontext.text: Match the following and choose the correct option.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each structure in angiosperm reproduction and seed anatomy corresponds to a specific developmental origin or physiological role.

Step 2: Evaluation
The aleurone layer is the proteinaceous outer layer of the endosperm in monocot seeds that provides nutrition and hydrolytic enzymes during germination. A parthenocarpic fruit is one formed without fertilization of the ovary. After fertilization, the ovule develops into a seed. Endosperm is the nutritive tissue formed as a result of triple fusion during double fertilization.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairs are: Aleurone layer — Nutrition; Parthenocarpic fruit — without fertilization; Ovule — Seed; Endosperm — Double fertilization.
